doc_summary: The paper shows that crowdsourced NLI datasets (SNLI, MultiNLI) contain annotation artifacts that let a hypothesis-only classifier beat baselines, so models' reported success is overestimated. It builds Hard/Easy splits to re-evaluate models and argues artifacts come from the annotation protocol and worker heuristics.

items.claim: prefers testing with a blind/ablated baseline that cannot access the intended signal over trusting headline benchmark scores because success may come from shortcuts rather than the target capability.
items.quote: Our finding demonstrates that it is possible to perform well on these datasets without modeling natural language inference.

items.claim: Distrusts high performance on a benchmark as evidence of capability, since models will exploit shortcuts in how the data was produced, 'gaming' the task.
items.quote: These findings coincide with ours, and strongly suggest that supervised models will exploit shortcuts in the data for gaming the benchmark, if such exist.

items.claim: Splits evaluation data into artifact-solvable (Easy) and artifact-resistant (Hard) subsets to see how much of the measured success depends on surface cues.
items.quote: we partition each NLI test set into two subsets: examples that the premise-oblivious model classified accurately are labeled Easy, and those it could not are Hard.

items.claim: Attributes surface regularities in generated data to the framing of the generation protocol and to the heuristics people adopt to produce items quickly, so the setup itself leaves detectable fingerprints.
items.quote: We conjecture that the framing of the annotation task has a significant effect on the language generation choices that crowd workers make when authoring hypotheses, producing certain patterns in the data.

items.claim: In a setup, avoid copying a single canonical example or template into the instructions to the generator instead of varying demonstrations, because it primes stereotyped patterns that become tells.
items.quote: This example likely primed the annotators, inducing the specific heuristics of replacing dog with animal and mentions of scenery with outdoors.

items.claim: Uses simple statistical analysis (PMI of words with labels, length distributions) to surface which lexical cues give away the label.
items.quote: We identify some of these heuristics by conducting a shallow statistical analysis of the data, focusing on lexical choice (Section 3.1) and sentence length (Section 3.2).

items.claim: prefers balancing artifacts across labels over filtering out artifact-bearing examples because filtering creates new artifacts and removes legitimate phenomena.
items.quote: Therefore, a better solution might not eliminate the artifacts altogether, but rather balance them across labels.

items.claim: Proposes future data collection that varies worker prompts and uses baseline or adversarial systems to flag examples relying on over-represented heuristics.
items.quote: Future strategies for reducing annotation artifacts might involve experimenting with the prompts or training given to crowd workers, e.g., to encourage a wide range of strategies, or incorporating baseline or adversarial systems that flag examples

items.claim: prefers claiming that the task remains open and benchmarks overestimate progress over declaring progress, and backs it by releasing harder test sets.
items.quote: We release the Hard SNLI and MultiNLI test sets, and encourage the community to use them for evaluating NLI models (in addition to the original benchmarks).

items.claim: Notes that individual cues are diverse and individually infrequent, so artifacts reflect multiple heuristics rather than a single tell, warning against over-reading any one cue.
items.quote: even the most discriminative words are not very frequent, indicating that the annotation artifacts are diverse, and that crowd workers tend to adopt multiple heuristics for generating new text.
